---
title: "Our approach"
description: "Where urban climate learning can break down and how the four questions connect."
---

<p class="page-deck">Urban climate knowledge is often represented as a linear path from evidence to action. In practice, evidence can fail to become visible, relevant, usable or deliverable, and its consequences may be measured in ways that prevent later learning.</p>

The lab's purpose is to study how urban climate knowledge is produced, compared, used and revised, so that cities can make better-grounded decisions without assuming that evidence applies unchanged across places.

## Where urban climate learning can break down

These six states are points at which the four-theme learning cycle can break down; they are not a second framework or a universal linear sequence.

<ol class="approach-states">
  <li><strong>Evidence is produced and made visible.</strong> Research, administrative, professional, community, local or Indigenous knowledge must exist and be reachable before it can enter a decision.</li>
  <li><strong>Relevance is judged rather than inferred.</strong> Visibility, popularity, proximity or apparent similarity does not by itself establish that evidence is informative for another setting.</li>
  <li><strong>New evidence is chosen for its potential to change understanding or decisions.</strong> Missing knowledge matters most where resolving it could alter an appraisal, distinguish mechanisms or expand who can learn.</li>
  <li><strong>Actors interpret evidence and institutions organise delivery.</strong> Professional judgement, values, authority, finance, capability, participation and coordination shape how evidence becomes action.</li>
  <li><strong>Consequences are distributed and evaluated.</strong> Benefits, burdens, risks and unintended effects occur across different people, places and periods, while appraisal determines which of them are counted.</li>
  <li><strong>Resulting knowledge revises later decisions.</strong> Outcomes expose unresolved questions, qualify prior assumptions and change what other places can plausibly learn.</li>
</ol>

## Illustration: expanding active travel {#illustration-expanding-active-travel}

::: {.notice}
**Hypothetical illustration.** This is a hypothetical illustration of the four questions, not a finding or policy recommendation.
:::

<ol class="cycle-illustration">
  <li><strong>Relevance across places.</strong> Evidence from other cities may be less relevant where travel patterns, street governance or climate differ.</li>
  <li><strong>New evidence.</strong> The most valuable new evidence may concern local uptake or distribution rather than another general case study.</li>
  <li><strong>Delivery.</strong> Outcomes depend on how authority, funding, maintenance and participation are organised.</li>
  <li><strong>Consequences and further learning.</strong> The programme could produce uneven effects on health, access, safety and affordability. Those consequences would revise what the first city, and other cities, can learn next.</li>
</ol>

## Commitments

- Contextual relevance should be examined rather than assumed.
- Evidence status and uncertainty should remain visible.
- A case may be useful without providing a universally transferable model.
- Failures and partial implementation may provide valuable knowledge.
- Local, professional, administrative, community and Indigenous knowledge should not be treated merely as inferior substitutes for published research.
- Questions about whose knowledge travels and whose outcomes are counted are questions of authority and justice.
- The lab does not seek context-free lists of universal best practices.
